newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians, Chechens talk to move peace deal further.
newsitem.headline: Russians, Chechens talk to move peace deal further.

text.p: Russian security tsar Alexander Lebed and Chechen rebel chief of staff Aslan Maskhadov on Thursday agreed measures to build on a shaky truce and political deal aimed at ending the 21-month-old conflict in Chechnya.

Lebed said after talks with Maskhadov in this village 25 km (15 miles) south of the regional capital Grozny that more Russian-rebel joint patrols would be sent in and new provisional bodies set up to maintain order in the city.

"We have agreed to increase the number of members of joint units," Lebed told reporters, referring to the groups comprising troops and rebels set up to patrol Grozny as Russian forces and separatist fighters withdraw.

"We agreed to set up joint law enforcement bodies because it is not enough to catch criminals. They should be put in prison, we need a prosecutor to deal with them and we need judges who will try them," Lebed added.
Lebed said that he and Maskhadov had agreed to make Grozny a demilitarised zone in which only the members of the joint patrols would be allowed to carry guns.

Maskhadov and Lebed, whom President Boris Yeltsin dispatched less than a month ago to end the Chechen war, struck a ceasefire deal two weeks ago and later agreed to defer a decision on the most sensitive issue of the conflict, Chechnya's future status.

The rebels, who celebrate the fifth anniversary of their unilateral declaration of independence on Friday, view Chechnya as a separate state. Moscow says the oil-rich region must stay part of the vast Russian Federation.

They agreed a fortnight ago that troops and rebels would leave Grozny, the scene of worst fighting since the start of conflict in late 1994 when Russia sent troops to quell Chechnya's independence bid.
"We have agreed to continue the peace process which is going ahead with difficulty and which has opponents on both sides and among criminal, bandit structures," Lebed said on Thursday.
Before starting the talks, Lebed specified two particularly tricky issues he said he hoped to tackle with Maskhadov.
Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying he was worried by reports of separatists seizing hostages and persecuting supporters of pro-Moscow authorities in the breakaway region.
Rebel leaders have denied the reports.

"Each time Alexander Ivanovich (Lebed) comes here full of negative and untrue information," Maskhadov told reporters after talks. "Now we have convinced him that we are not going to persecute, jail, rob or kill anyone."
Lebed is Yeltsin's representative in Chechnya, but the 65-year-old president, on holiday near Moscow, has not publicly backed his peace deal.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has given the accord his guarded approval and RIA news agency said on Thursday that Yeltsin had recorded a television interview including comments about Chechnya. It would be shown later in the day, RIA said.
Another key question is the shape of a future Chechen administration.
Lebed, quoted by Itar-Tass news agency, said he favoured a coalition government comprising separatist leaders, members of the Moscow-backed Chechen administration and members of the Chechen diaspora.

Doku Zavgayev, the Moscow-backed leader of Chechnya, told Ekho Moskvy radio he was ready to broaden his government to include "Dudayevists" -- separatists loyal to former rebel leader Dzhokhar Dudayev.
Dudayev was killed in a rocket attack in April but the there are wild rumours in Chechnya that he could return to Grozny to mark independence day.
